context: 0:About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. context: 47: Radiation therapy Radiation therapy (RT) is a type of cancer treatment that uses beams of intense energy – from electrons (beams), photons (high-energy x-rays), or protons (charged particles) -- to kill cancer cells. Radiation therapy usually involves 5 daily brief treatments per week over 3 to 7 weeks. Radiation treatments should be given by a practicing radiation oncologist (a doctor who is an expert in radiation treatment). Types of radiation therapy There are two general types of radiation therapy that can be used to treat CSCC: external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy. In EBRT, a beam of radiation is directed at the tumor from a machine. The two most common types of external beam radiation for CSCC are electrons and photons. Electrons are used to treat superficial tumors. Photons are used to treat deeper, more invasive tumors. In brachytherapy, a radiation source is placed close to or in direct contact with the tumor for a short period of time. Radiation therapy usually involves 5 daily brief treatments per week over 3 to 7 weeks. Radiation treatments should be given by a practicing radiation oncologist (a doctor who is an expert in radiation treatment). In EBRT, a beam of radiation is directed at the tumor from a machine. The two most common types of external beam radiation for CSCC are electrons and photons. Electrons are used to treat superficial tumors. Photons are used to treat deeper, more invasive tumors. In brachytherapy, a radiation source is placed close to or in direct contact with the tumor for a short period of time. Although there are different treatment options for primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, the treatment approach is often a two-step process. The first step is the induction phase, which aims to wipe out all lymphoma cells or as many as possible. The goal of the second step, the consolidation phase, is to destroy any cancer cells that may remain in the body after the first phase. Testing of your leukemia cells can gather specific information about your leukemia to help guide treatment. AML genetic changes AML cells can have changes in genes and chromosomes. Mutation testing looks for these changes or abnormalities that are unique to AML cells. Examples of such changes are called deletion, insertion, inversion, amplification, translocation (rearrangement), and point mutation. Amplification – When a part or whole chromosome or gene is increased (for example, duplicated) Deletion – When part of a chromosome or gene is missing such as del(5q) Insertion – When a new part of a chromosome or gene is included Inversion – Switching of parts within one chromosome such as inv(16) and inv(3) Point mutation – When part of a gene is changed Chromosome translocation and gene rearrangement – Switching of parts between 2 chromosomes. There’s no single drug or procedure that’s best for treating primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. The best treatment is the one that works best for you. Treatment options include corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. Receiving treatment in a clinical trial is also a recommended option. Therapies are often combined to treat cancer. For example, chemotherapy may be given with an immunotherapy drug, or several chemotherapy drugs may be given together. Chemotherapy is also an essential part of having a stem cell rescue. Surgery is not normally an option. Because primary CNS lymphoma usually develops deep within the brain tissue, removing it with surgery is risky and may be more harmful than helpful. Treatment is usually given in phases (which are discussed in the next chapter). Clinical trial NCCN experts recommend that everyone with primary CNS lymphoma consider joining a clinical trial for treatment. A clinical trial is a type of medical research study. Clinical trials are a key way to assess new treatment approaches. After being developed and tested in a laboratory, potential new ways of fighting cancer need to be studied in people.

Two such conditions include Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). People born with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. FAP causes hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum. The polyps start as benign growths, but over time can become invasive colon cancer. Bone is a living tissue made of cells (osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts), calcium, phosphate, hydroxyapatite (a bone mineral), and collagen. New bone formation, known as ossification, starts in the womb and ends during adolescence, between 10 and 19 years of age. Ossification is complete when the skeleton is done growing. Once ossification is complete, bone is continuously being replaced by a process called remodeling. Remodeling breaks down and rebuilds bone and helps maintain normal calcium levels in the body. When calcium is needed, cells called osteoclasts break down bone. This releases calcium into the bloodstream. At the same time, bone-forming cells called osteoblasts create bone from calcium in the bloodstream. Some types of bone cancer can interrupt this process. Metastasis Unlike normal cells, cancer cells can spread and form tumors in other parts of the body called metastases. In this process, cancer cells break away from the first (primary) tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites. Once in other sites, cancer cells may form secondary tumors. Since cancer cells can spread through the blood, it is still possible to develop metastases even when the axillary lymph nodes are negative for cancer. Cancer that has spread to a nearby body part such as the axillary lymph nodes is called a local metastasis. It might be referred to as locoregional disease or locally advanced. Cancer that has spread to a body part far from the primary tumor is called a distant metastasis. The head and neck contain a network of more than 300 nodes. They are bound together with muscles, nerves, and blood and lymph vessels. Head and neck cancers sometimes spread to neck lymph nodes. Regional lymph nodes are found near the tumor. Cancer found in a regional lymph node is a lymph node metastasis. This is different than a distant metastasis, which is found outside the neck. Oral mucosa The oral mucosa is the mucous membrane lining the inside of the mouth and lips. It is made up of 2 layers. Epithelium – The surface layer containing stratified squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells. Lamina propria – The bottom layer of connective tissue. Nonkeratinized squamous epithelium covers the soft palate, inner lips, inner cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and area underneath the tongue. Mutation testing looks for these changes or abnormalities that are unique to AML cells. Examples of such changes are called deletion, insertion, inversion, amplification, translocation (rearrangement), and point mutation. Amplification – When a part or whole chromosome or gene is increased (for example, duplicated) Deletion – When part of a chromosome or gene is missing such as del(5q) Insertion – When a new part of a chromosome or gene is included Inversion – Switching of parts within one chromosome such as inv(16) and inv(3) Point mutation – When part of a gene is changed Chromosome translocation and gene rearrangement – Switching of parts between 2 chromosomes. When described at the chromosome level, it is called a translocation. When described at the gene level, it is called rearrangement. Bone marrow is the sponge-like tissue in the center of most bones. Inside your bone marrow are early blood-forming cells called blood (hematopoietic) stem cells. All types of blood cells are created from blood stem cells. At any given time, the bone marrow will have cells in various stages of development, from very immature to almost fully mature. This process is called differentiation. After a blood stem cell develops into a red blood cell, white blood cell, or platelet, it is released into your bloodstream as needed. The role of blood stem cells is to make cells called intermediaries that will become red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. These intermediaries are called progenitor cells or precursor cells. There are different types of progenitor cells: Lymphoid progenitor cells form into lymphoblasts that mature into lymphocytes. Myeloid progenitor cells form into myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells. ALL is thought to arise from stem cells that make an increased amount of lymphoid progenitor cells. Radiation damages the ovaries and causes them to stop producing hormones needed for natural pregnancy. Supportive care refers to a range of care and resources often needed by patients with metastatic cancer. Hospice care, access to pain specialists, and emotional and spiritual support are all components of supportive care. Because metastatic cancer cannot be cured, the main goal of supportive care is to make you more comfortable and to help keep the cancer under control. Supportive care may also help you live longer and feel better overall. When used for advanced cancers, supportive care is often called palliative care. You may also consider enrolling in a clinical trial. Ask your treatment team if there is an open clinical trial that you can join. Advance care planning Talking with your doctor about your prognosis can help with treatment planning. If the cancer cannot be controlled or cured, a care plan for the end of life can be made. Bone marrow is the sponge-like tissue in the center of most bones. Inside your bone marrow are early blood-forming cells called blood (hematopoietic) stem cells. All types of blood cells are created from blood stem cells. At any given time, the bone marrow will have cells in various stages of development, from very immature to almost fully mature. This process is called differentiation. After a blood stem cell develops into a red blood cell, white blood cell, or platelet, it is released into your bloodstream as needed. The role of blood stem cells is to make cells called intermediaries that will become red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. These intermediaries are called progenitor cells or precursor cells. There are different types of progenitor cells: Lymphoid progenitor cells form into lymphoblasts that mature into lymphocytes. Supportive care refers to a range of care and resources often needed by patients with metastatic cancer. Hospice care, access to pain specialists, and emotional and spiritual support are all components of supportive care. Because metastatic cancer cannot be cured, the main goal of supportive care is to make you more comfortable and to help keep the cancer under control. Supportive care may also help you live longer and feel better overall. When used for advanced cancers, supportive care is often called palliative care. You may also consider enrolling in a clinical trial. Ask your treatment team if there is an open clinical trial that you can join. Advance care planning Talking with your doctor about your prognosis can help with treatment planning. If the cancer cannot be controlled or cured, a care plan for the end of life can be made. There are many benefits to advance care planning, including: Knowing what to expect Making the most of your time Lowering the stress of caregivers Having your wishes followed Having a better quality of life

In brachytherapy, a radiation source is placed close to or in direct contact with the tumor for a short period of time. The rest of the colon has 4 main sections: the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. The term colorectal cancer is used to describe cancers that form in either the colon or rectum. Supportive care refers to a range of care and resources often needed by patients with metastatic cancer. Hospice care, access to pain specialists, and emotional and spiritual support are all components of supportive care. Because metastatic cancer cannot be cured, the main goal of supportive care is to make you more comfortable and to help keep the cancer under control. Supportive care may also help you live longer and feel better overall. When used for advanced cancers, supportive care is often called palliative care. You may also consider enrolling in a clinical trial. Ask your treatment team if there is an open clinical trial that you can join. Advance care planning Talking with your doctor about your prognosis can help with treatment planning. If the cancer cannot be controlled or cured, a care plan for the end of life can be made. This is called metastatic colon cancer to the liver. There is more than one type of primary liver cancer in adults. The most common type is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). How liver cancer spreads Liver cancer can spread in many ways. It can spread directly through the liver. It can also spread to an area far from the primary tumor called a distant metastasis. Bone is a living tissue made of cells (osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts), calcium, phosphate, hydroxyapatite (a bone mineral), and collagen. New bone formation, known as ossification, starts in the womb and ends during adolescence, between 10 and 19 years of age. Ossification is complete when the skeleton is done growing. Once ossification is complete, bone is continuously being replaced by a process called remodeling. Remodeling breaks down and rebuilds bone and helps maintain normal calcium levels in the body. When calcium is needed, cells called osteoclasts break down bone. This releases calcium into the bloodstream. At the same time, bone-forming cells called osteoblasts create bone from calcium in the bloodstream. Some types of bone cancer can interrupt this process. PSA is a protein made inside the prostate gland. Its job is to help semen transport sperm. All prostate cells, both normal cells and cancer cells, make PSA. context: 871: in Chapter What causes bladder cancer? Many people wonder why they got cancer. Cancer experts don’t know exactly what causes bladder cells to grow out of control. What they do know is that bladder cancer and other cancers start with abnormal changes (mutations) in the genes of cells. Genes are tiny parts of a cell that carry the instructions for how cells behave. These instructions also control how new cells are made. Sometimes, mutations can mix up these instructions. This can turn normal cells into cancer cells. In most people with bladder cancer, these mutations aren’t passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Many people live full, healthy lives with only one kidney. Kidney cancer Kidney cancer starts in the tissues of the kidneys. Almost all kidney cancers are carcinomas. This is called renal cell carcinoma (RCC). About 9 out of 10 kidney cancers are RCCs. RCC may appear as multiple tumors in one kidney or involve both kidneys. Because it is the most common type, RCC is often simply referred to as kidney cancer. RCC is the focus of this book. There are other, less common cancers that can arise in the kidney. Metastatic prostate cancer may spread to the lymph nodes, bones, liver, lungs, and other organs. This book is all about advanced-stage prostate cancer. Cancer that grows from the prostate gland to nearby areas such as lymph nodes, but no farther, is called regional prostate cancer. (It’s also called locally advanced prostate cancer. This book will call it regional prostate cancer to avoid confusion between localized and locally advanced.) Cancer that spreads beyond the prostate to other parts of the body is called distant metastatic prostate cancer or simply metastatic prostate cancer. How does prostate cancer spread? Cancer cells use the bloodstream like a highway to travel to distant areas in the body. Cancer cells can also spread through the lymphatic system. The lymphatic system is a network of organs and vessels that fights infections and circulates a clear fluid called lymph throughout the body. A normal and important part of the lymphatic system are the lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small, disease-fighting clusters that filter lymph fluid to remove germs. Lymph vessels and nodes are found everywhere in the body. Some patients have advanced-stage prostate cancer when they’re first diagnosed. Others develop advanced-stage cancer

Often, hormone therapy is combined with one or more other therapies. Combining therapies can be more effective than using either therapy alone. key word in ADT is “deprivation”—this therapy “deprives” (starves) the cancer of its main fuel: androgens. This can shrink the tumor or slow tumor growth for a while. You might hear the term “castration” used when describing prostate cancer or its treatment. This term describes a drastic reduction of testosterone. Castration can be done with hormone-lowering medication or by surgical removal of one or both testicles (orchiectomy). Though orchiectomy is a surgical procedure, it’s still considered hormone therapy because it removes the primary source of testosterone: the testicles. While drug hormone therapy can be reversed when the medication is stopped, orchiectomy is permanent and can’t be reversed. 469: common these days because systemic Hormone therapy Hormone therapy is a systemic (whole-body) treatment that adds, blocks, or removes hormones. A hormone is a natural chemical made by a gland in the body. Its job is to activate cells or organs. Male hormones are called androgens. The main androgen is testosterone. Most of the testosterone in the body is made by the testicles. Testosterone helps produce sperm, among other functions. But testosterone also helps prostate cancer grow. A type of hormone therapy called androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) can stop your body from making testosterone or block cancer cells from using testosterone. The What is ADT? Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) brings testosterone down to a very low level. Hormone therapies for prostate cancer include luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists and LHRH antagonists, both of which cause the testicles to stop making testosterone. You may have heard of leuprolide (Lupron), a commonly used LHRH agonist or degarelix (Firmagon), a commonly used LHRH antagonist. Most LHRH agonists and LHRH antagonists are injections. Surgical techniques may involve standard excision or Mohs micrographic surgery, especially for high-risk or recurrent cases. In situations where surgery is not feasible or if the cancer is not completely removed, radiation therapy may be considered as an alternative or adjunct treatment. Systemic therapy, such as platinum-based chemotherapy or immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors, may be used in advanced cases, when radiation is not suitable, or when the cancer has spread. The choice of treatment depends on factors such as tumor size, location, risk of recurrence, and patient health.

ground_truth: The diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma involves a combination of clinical evaluation and specialized diagnostic tests. A neurological exam is performed to assess neurological function and identify deficits. Imaging studies, particularly MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast, are the most useful for detecting lesions characteristic of primary CNS lymphoma; CT scans may be used if MRI is unavailable. If imaging suggests lymphoma, a stereotactic biopsy is the standard and most definitive diagnostic procedure, allowing for precise sampling of tumor tissue for pathological confirmation. Additional diagnostic methods include blood tests (such as HIV testing, as immunosuppression is a risk factor), a thorough eye examination to detect ocular involvement, and lumbar puncture to analyze cerebrospinal fluid for malignant cells. Each method plays a specific role: imaging identifies and localizes lesions, biopsy confirms the diagnosis and guides treatment, and ancillary tests assess disease extent and associated risk factors.

ground_truth: Major risk factors for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) include chronic sun exposure, especially in fair-skinned individuals, and the use of indoor tanning devices. The overall risk category is determined by the highest risk factor present, and this stratification guides treatment decisions and prognosis.

Photodynamic therapy involves applying a light-sensitive drug to the skin, which is then activated by exposure to specific wavelengths of light to destroy abnormal cells. Cryotherapy uses extreme cold, typically liquid nitrogen, to freeze and destroy precancerous and cancerous cells. Topical therapies are medications applied directly to the skin and include 5-fluorouracil (a topical chemotherapy), imiquimod (an immune response modifier), calcipotriene (a vitamin D analog that activates the skin’s immune system), tirbanibulin (a microtubule inhibitor that targets rapidly dividing cells), and diclofenac (a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug). These treatments are considered superficial therapies, as they primarily affect the top layer of the skin and are suitable for early or superficial lesions.

In the chronic phase, there is an overproduction of mature and maturing myeloid cells, particularly granulocytes, in the blood and bone marrow, often accompanied by abnormal counts of platelets and sometimes red blood cells. The blast phase represents an advanced stage of CML, characterized by a marked increase in immature cells called blasts, which can be of myeloid or lymphoid lineage. This phase involves a significant accumulation of these immature progenitor cells, leading to more aggressive disease and symptoms, and the specific lineage of blasts (myeloid or lymphoid) can influence treatment decisions.

Treatment for stage 4 is generally focused on systemic therapies such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy, rather than surgery.

ground_truth: The primary treatment options for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) vary depending on the stage of the disease. For early-stage NSCLC (stage 1), surgery is often the preferred treatment to remove the tumor, provided the patient is a suitable candidate. In some cases where surgery is not possible, radiation therapy may be used as an alternative. For locally advanced NSCLC (stages 2 and 3), treatment may involve a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, and chemoradiation (the use of chemotherapy and radiation together) to improve outcomes. Supportive care is an important component at all stages, aiming to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life, and has been shown to extend and enhance life for people with lung cancer. Additionally, participation in clinical trials is encouraged, as these offer access to investigational therapies and new approaches to treatment. The choice of treatment is individualized based on the patient's overall health, cancer stage, and preferences, and is best determined in collaboration with a multidisciplinary care team.

ground_truth: Lung nodules play a critical role in the detection and diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). These small masses of tissue in the lungs are often first identified through imaging studies such as chest X-rays or CT scans. While most lung nodules are benign and may result from infections, scar tissue, or other non-cancerous conditions, some can be malignant and indicative of NSCLC. To determine the nature of a lung nodule, a multidisciplinary team—including pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, and thoracic surgeons—will assess the patient's risk factors, review imaging findings, and may recommend additional imaging or a biopsy. Biopsy of the nodule is essential to confirm malignancy and establish a definitive diagnosis of NSCLC. Early detection and accurate diagnosis of malignant lung nodules are crucial for timely treatment planning and improved outcomes.

ground_truth: The main types of treatments for colon cancer include both surgical and non-surgical approaches. Surgical treatments involve procedures such as polypectomy, which removes polyps during colonoscopy and is often sufficient for early-stage or malignant polyps; colectomy, which is the surgical removal of the cancerous portion of the colon and is standard for non-metastatic colon cancer; and colostomy, which diverts stool through an abdominal stoma if reconnection of the colon is not possible. Non-surgical treatments include chemotherapy, which is typically recommended after colectomy for all stage 3 and some stage 2 colon cancers, and is administered in cycles to target cancer cells throughout the body. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors, such as pembrolizumab or nivolumab (with or without ipilimumab), is preferred for patients whose tumors have mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H). In certain cases, radiation therapy may also be used, particularly for unresectable cancers. Treatment selection is guided by tumor stage, biomarker status, and individual patient factors.

Although there are different treatment options for primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, the treatment approach is often a two-step process. The first step is the induction phase, which aims to wipe out all lymphoma cells or as many as possible. The goal of the second step, the consolidation phase, is to destroy any cancer cells that may remain in the body after the first phase. Consolidation is also for preventing the lymphoma from returning. Induction The first (induction) phase of treatment can last several months. Treatment typically requires multiple courses of chemotherapy, which are given while in the hospital. ground_truth: The main treatment options for mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) include chemotherapy as the primary approach. If the tumor cells express appropriate markers, rituximab may be added to chemotherapy to form chemoimmunotherapy. Involved-site radiation therapy (ISRT) can be considered for patients with localized disease. The choice of treatment depends on disease extent and individual patient factors, and management is best conducted at specialized cancer centers due to the complexity and rarity of MGZL.

ground_truth: The diagnosis of mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) requires expert hematopathologist review due to its overlapping features with other lymphomas. Essential diagnostic methods include thorough histopathological examination of a biopsy from the mediastinal mass. Key histopathological features are the presence of a large mediastinal mass and identification of Reed-Sternberg cells, which are large, abnormal lymphocytes that may contain more than one nucleus and resemble those seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. The tumor cells in MGZL can vary in size and appearance, further necessitating specialized pathological assessment to distinguish MGZL from related entities such as primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL).

When gray zone lymphoma presents outside the mediastinum—such as with bone marrow or extranodal involvement, and in cases of advanced-stage disease—it is classified and diagnosed as DLBCL-NOS. According to current guidelines, any gray zone lymphoma with extra-mediastinal disease should be diagnosed as DLBCL-NOS.

HPV is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection (STI). Most sexually active people have or had HPV at one point. Most are unaware that they are or were infected. In most people, the immune system gets rid of (“clears”) HPV from the body. In other people, the virus causes long-term cell changes that develop into cancer. The progression to cancer often occurs decades after the initial infection. Experts are still learning why one person gets cervical cancer and another does not. Other types of cancer caused by HPV include anal, head and neck, penile, vaginal, and vulvar cancers. There are more than 100 types (strains) of HPV. Key biomarkers and genetic alterations include PD-L1 expression, microsatellite instability (MSI), mismatch repair deficiency (MMR), tumor mutational burden (TMB), HER2 amplification, RET gene fusion, and NTRK gene fusion. Radiation damages the ovaries and causes them to stop producing hormones needed for natural pregnancy. Ovarian transposition is a surgery that moves one or both ovaries out of the range of the radiation beam. The medical name for this procedure is oophoropexy. ground_truth: For patients with early-stage cervical cancer who wish to preserve fertility, several options are available. Fertility-sparing surgery, such as trachelectomy or cone biopsy, may be considered for cancers confined to the cervix (typically stage 1) and in the absence of certain risk factors. These procedures aim to remove the cancer while preserving the uterus and ovaries, allowing for the possibility of future natural pregnancy. Ovarian transposition (oophoropexy) can be performed to move the ovaries out of the radiation field if pelvic radiation is planned, helping to preserve ovarian function. Additionally, egg (oocyte) freezing prior to treatment is an option for those at risk of losing fertility due to surgery or radiation. Surrogacy may also be considered for patients who are unable to carry a pregnancy after treatment. Consultation with a reproductive endocrinologist is recommended to discuss the most appropriate fertility preservation strategies based on individual circumstances and cancer stage.

Supportive care refers to a range of care and resources often needed by patients with metastatic cancer. Hospice care, access to pain specialists, and emotional and spiritual support are all components of supportive care. Because metastatic cancer cannot be cured, the main goal of supportive care is to make you more comfortable and to help keep the cancer under control. Supportive care may also help you live longer and feel better overall. When used for advanced cancers, supportive care is often called palliative care. Your treatment options will depend on the extent of the cancer and other factors. Surgery Surgery is often the main treatment for earlystage cervical cancer. The types of surgery that may be used are described below. Removing only a portion of the cervix may be an option for the earliest stage of cervical cancer. Minimally invasive (also called laparoscopic) surgery involves making only a few small cuts into your body. There is usually less pain and scarring compared to surgery that uses a larger cut through the abdomen. The time it takes to recover is also usually shorter. ground_truth: Therapeutic options for metastatic cervical cancer include systemic therapies such as platinum-based chemotherapy (e.g., cisplatin or carboplatin, often combined with paclitaxel or topotecan), targeted therapy (such as bevacizumab, which may be added to chemotherapy regimens), and immunotherapy. The use of immunotherapy, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab, is guided by biomarker testing (e.g., PD-L1 positivity, TMB-H, or MSI-H/dMMR status). For patients whose tumors lack these biomarkers, other immunotherapies (such as tisotumab vedotin-tftv or cemiplimab) may be considered. Supportive and palliative care are important components of management to improve quality of life. Clinical trials are recommended as an option at all stages of metastatic cervical cancer, offering access to novel therapies and combinations. Treatment selection is individualized based on prior therapies, biomarker status, and patient factors.

ground_truth: The gallbladder and bile ducts are organized anatomically into five main histological layers, arranged from the innermost to the outermost as follows: (1) the epithelium, which is a thin, moist layer of cells lining the lumen; (2) the lamina propria, a connective tissue layer located just beneath the epithelium; (3) the muscularis, a layer of smooth muscle tissue; (4) the perimuscular fibrous tissue, which is connective tissue surrounding the muscle layer; and (5) the serosa, an outer membrane also known as the serous membrane or visceral peritoneum, which covers the external surface of the gallbladder and bile ducts.

The grade of FL is important because it guides treatment decisions and helps predict disease behavior.

ground_truth: Treatment decisions and clinical management for follicular lymphoma (FL) are primarily determined by the grade and cell type of the lymphoma. Accurate diagnosis involves a combination of blood tests, biopsies, immunophenotyping, and imaging studies to assess the extent and characteristics of the disease. Not all patients with FL require immediate treatment; some may be managed with observation, especially if they are asymptomatic and have a low tumor burden. The grade of FL, which is based on the proportion of centroblasts (large B cells) present, guides therapy: grades 1, 2, and 3A are often treated as classic FL, while grade 3B is managed as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) due to its more aggressive nature. Uncommon FL (uFL), which may lack the typical t(14;18) translocation or have unusual pathological features, is generally treated in the same way as classic FL. In addition, transformed FL, where the disease evolves into a more aggressive lymphoma such as DLBCL, requires a different treatment approach. Thus, individualized management is based on disease grade, cell type, clinical presentation, and the presence or absence of symptoms.

The standard screening methods include an abdominal ultrasound and a blood test for alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), both performed every 6 months. The ultrasound uses sound waves to create images of the liver to detect any abnormal growths, while the AFP test measures a protein that can be elevated in liver cancer. If the ultrasound identifies nodules 10 mm or larger, or if AFP levels are elevated, further diagnostic testing is warranted. For smaller nodules or negative findings, repeat screening is advised at regular intervals. The goal of this screening protocol is to detect liver cancer at an early, more treatable stage in high-risk individuals.

These samples are then reviewed by a pathologist to determine if cancer is present and to identify the specific type of thyroid cancer. ground_truth: Recommended follow-up and surveillance after thyroid cancer treatment depend on the type of surgery and risk of recurrence. After total thyroidectomy, short-term follow-up includes a physical exam, blood tests (thyroid-stimulating hormone [TSH], thyroglobulin [Tg], and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies [Tg ab]), and a neck ultrasound 6–12 months postoperatively. If radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy was given, a whole-body RAI scan may be performed, especially in high-risk patients or those with abnormal test results. For patients who have undergone lobectomy, follow-up consists of a physical exam, TSH blood test, and neck ultrasound 6–12 months after surgery; Tg testing is not useful in this setting. Long-term surveillance for all patients with no evidence of disease includes periodic physical exams, blood tests (TSH, and for total thyroidectomy, Tg and Tg ab), and periodic neck ultrasound. If there is suspicion of recurrence, additional laboratory tests, TSH-stimulated testing, or imaging such as CT or MRI may be indicated. Surveillance is continued long-term, as recurrence can occur years after initial treatment.

Genetic cancer risk testing, typically performed on blood or saliva, identifies inherited (germline) mutations that may increase the risk of bone cancer and other malignancies, informing both patient management and family counseling. Together, these tests assist in risk assessment, guide personalized treatment decisions, and may influence prognosis.

ground_truth: The main diagnostic methods and laboratory tests used to diagnose acute myeloid leukemia (AML) include a combination of blood tests, bone marrow evaluation, specialized laboratory analyses, and imaging studies. Initial laboratory tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC) with differential to assess for abnormal white blood cells, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, as well as a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), uric acid, and blood clotting tests to evaluate organ function and metabolic status. Definitive diagnosis requires a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, which are examined for the presence of ≥20% myeloblasts, although diagnosis can sometimes be made with fewer blasts if specific genetic abnormalities are present. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping are performed on blood or bone marrow samples to characterize the immunologic profile of the leukemic cells. Molecular and cytogenetic testing—including karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), next-generation sequencing (NGS), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)—are used to identify chromosomal abnormalities and gene mutations that inform prognosis and guide therapy. Imaging studies such as CT, MRI, and PET/CT may be used to assess for extramedullary disease or complications, and additional tests like lumbar puncture or heart function assessment may be performed based on clinical indications.

ground_truth: Before starting treatment for AML, it is important to discuss the potential impact of chemotherapy and other therapies on fertility, as these treatments can cause temporary or permanent infertility. Patients who may want to have children in the future should be referred to a fertility or reproductive specialist to discuss preservation options, such as sperm banking or egg/embryo freezing, prior to initiating therapy. The risk of fertility impairment depends on factors such as age, treatment type, dose, and duration. Additionally, patients should be counseled on the need for effective contraception during and after treatment, as cancer therapies can harm a developing fetus. Early discussion with the care team ensures that patients are informed about their options and can make decisions that align with their future family planning goals.

These symptoms are often categorized as gastrointestinal (such as bloating, trouble eating, feeling full quickly, and constipation), genitourinary (urinary urgency or frequency), gynecologic (pain during sex), and constitutional (fatigue, unexplained weight loss). Symptoms are more likely to be related to ovarian cancer if they are new (less than one year in duration), occur more than 12 days per month, and become more severe over time.

This type of doctor is an expert in surgery and chemotherapy for gynecologic cancers. Your care team may also include a medical oncologist. ground_truth: Recommended surveillance strategies after initial treatment for ovarian cancer include regular physical and pelvic examinations, typically every 2 to 4 months for the first 2 years, every 3 to 6 months for the next 3 years, and annually after 5 years. Monitoring of CA-125 or other tumor markers is advised if these markers were elevated at diagnosis. ground_truth: The main diagnostic methods and biomarkers used in the diagnosis and management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) include several laboratory and imaging tests. Diagnosis typically begins with a complete blood count (CBC) with differential, which often reveals elevated white blood cell counts and may show low red blood cell or platelet counts. Flow cytometry is used for immunophenotyping to identify CLL cells by their characteristic surface proteins, such as CD20, CD200, and LEF1. Additional tests may include lymph node or bone marrow biopsies if further tissue characterization is needed. Biomarker testing is essential for prognosis and treatment planning: fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detects chromosomal abnormalities such as 17p deletion; DNA sequencing identifies mutations in the TP53 and IGHV genes; and karyotype analysis assesses for complex chromosomal changes. Measurement of beta-2 microglobulin in the blood serves as a biomarker for disease activity and prognosis. Imaging studies, such as diagnostic CT scans, may be used to evaluate lymph node involvement and disease extent prior to treatment. These diagnostic and biomarker assessments guide both the initial diagnosis and ongoing management of CLL.

ground_truth: A major complication of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is Richter transformation, in which CLL transforms into a more aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or, less frequently, Hodgkin lymphoma. This transformation is characterized by a sudden worsening of symptoms, including rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, new or worsening B symptoms (such as fevers, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss), and a more aggressive clinical course. In addition to Richter transformation, CLL can also lead to complications such as increased risk of infections due to impaired immune function, anemia, and low platelet counts as abnormal B cells crowd out healthy blood cells.

ground_truth: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) are considered the same disease, but they are distinguished by their primary sites of involvement and clinical presentation. CLL primarily affects the blood and bone marrow, with abnormal B lymphocytes circulating in the bloodstream and accumulating in the marrow. In contrast, SLL involves the same malignant B cells but is mainly found in the lymph nodes and spleen, with minimal involvement of the blood (fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells per microliter). Both conditions can cause lymph node or spleen enlargement, but CLL is typically diagnosed through blood tests, while SLL is often identified by lymph node biopsy. Despite these differences in presentation, the underlying cancer cells are the same, and treatment approaches are similar for both CLL and SLL.

ground_truth: Assessment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) at diagnosis and during follow-up commonly involves several laboratory and imaging studies. A complete blood count (CBC) with differential is used to evaluate white blood cell, red blood cell, and platelet counts, which are often abnormal in CLL. Flow cytometry is performed to confirm the presence of monoclonal B lymphocytes and to characterize their immunophenotype. A comprehensive metabolic panel assesses kidney and liver function, which is important for treatment planning. Beta-2 microglobulin testing serves as a biomarker for disease activity and prognosis. Diagnostic CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis may be used to assess lymph node involvement and the extent of disease. Additional tests, such as biomarker studies (e.g., FISH for chromosomal abnormalities, DNA sequencing for gene mutations), may also be performed to guide treatment decisions.

Imaging studies such as CT scan, MRI, PET/CT, and ultrasound are used to determine the size and extent of the tumor, involvement of lymph nodes, and possible distant metastases. Scoping procedures, including endoscopy, laryngoscopy, nasolaryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy, and panendoscopy, allow direct visualization of the tumor and surrounding structures. Tissue sampling through biopsy—such as fine-needle aspiration (FNA), core needle biopsy (CNB), or endoscopic biopsy—is required for definitive diagnosis and may also be used for biomarker testing, including HPV (p16) status. Staging is performed using the AJCC TNM system, which evaluates tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M), and may be further refined after surgical removal of the tumor and lymph nodes.

Follicular lymphoma Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). It is a slow-dividing, slow-growing B-cell lymphoma that typically forms tumors in lymph nodes. However, FL can form tumors in other parts of the body such as the bone marrow. This is called extranodal (outside of the lymph node) disease. Not everyone with FL needs treatment right away. How does FL develop? In lymph nodes, temporary germinal centers (GCs) form in response to an immune stressor such as infection or inflammation. This is normal. But, when cells within germinal centers grow without proper regulation, it can develop into FL. In FL, excess amounts of abnormal B lymphocytes group together to form clusters (follicles) in the lymph nodes. ground_truth: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas (CBCLs) typically present as indolent or slow-growing lesions on the skin, most often appearing as nodules or papules that may resemble small pimples. The most common types include primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma, primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma, and primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type. CBCLs are generally characterized by their slow progression and localized skin involvement.

ground_truth: The main subtypes of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in children are B-cell ALL (B-ALL) and T-cell ALL (T-ALL). B-ALL originates from B-cell lymphocytes and is the more common subtype. In some cases, B-cell lymphoblasts primarily grow in the lymph nodes rather than the bone marrow, a condition known as B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-LL or B-LBL). T-ALL arises from T-cell lymphocytes and is less common. A distinguishing feature of T-ALL is its tendency to cause enlargement of the thymus, which can lead to breathing difficulties due to pressure on the windpipe and blood vessels. When T-cell lymphoblasts predominantly grow in the thymus, this is referred to as T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LL or T-LBL). The subtypes are further characterized by the type and maturity of the lymphocyte involved, as well as specific genetic or chromosomal changes within the leukemia cells.

ground_truth: In children, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) commonly involves the bone marrow and blood, but can also affect other sites such as the testicles and central nervous system (CNS). Disease sites may include lymph nodes and, in the case of T-cell ALL, the thymus. T-cell ALL can cause an enlarged thymus, which may lead to breathing difficulties due to compression of the windpipe and nearby blood vessels. ground_truth: Bladder-preserving approaches in bladder cancer include trimodal therapy and radiation-based treatments. Trimodal therapy consists of three components: transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) to remove all visible cancer, followed by external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and concurrent chemotherapy (chemoradiation). This approach aims to eradicate the tumor while preserving the bladder, and is considered for select patients as an alternative to radical cystectomy. Radiation therapy (EBRT) can also be used alone or in combination with chemotherapy (chemoradiation) to enhance treatment effectiveness. The choice of therapy depends on tumor characteristics and patient factors, and these approaches are designed to maintain bladder function while achieving cancer control.

ground_truth: The major subtypes of kidney cancer include renal cell carcinoma (RCC), urothelial carcinoma, Wilms tumor, and renal sarcoma. RCC is the most common type, accounting for about 90% of kidney cancers, and arises from the cells lining the renal tubules. Histologically, RCC is classified into clear cell RCC (the most common subtype, characterized by pale or clear cells under the microscope), and non-clear cell RCC, which includes papillary RCC (with finger-like projections), chromophobe RCC (with larger, pale cells), collecting duct RCC, renal medullary carcinoma, clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, and ELOC-mutated RCC. Sarcomatoid features can develop in any RCC subtype and are associated with more aggressive disease. Urothelial carcinoma originates from the lining of the renal pelvis and ureter, Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) typically occurs in children, and renal sarcoma arises from the kidney's connective tissues or blood vessels. Histological classification is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning.

ground_truth: Anal cancer is staged using the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM system, which assesses tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M). Stage 0 (carcinoma in situ or anal dysplasia) refers to abnormal cells confined to the surface layer, also called high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) or high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL). Stage I is defined by a tumor 2 cm or smaller (T1) with no spread to lymph nodes (N0) or distant sites (M0). Stage II is divided into IIA (tumor >2 cm but ≤5 cm, T2) and IIB (tumor >5 cm, T3), both without lymph node or distant spread. Stage III is subdivided: IIIA involves tumors ≤5 cm with spread to nearby lymph nodes (N1), IIIB involves invasion into adjacent organs (such as the vagina, urethra, or bladder) without lymph node involvement, and IIIC includes larger tumors or those invading nearby organs with lymph node involvement. Stage IV indicates distant metastasis, meaning the cancer has spread beyond the pelvis to organs such as the liver or lungs. Accurate staging guides treatment decisions and prognosis.

IMRT is an advanced radiation technique recommended for treating anal cancer. It can limit radiation exposure to areas near the tumor, such as the genitals, small intestine and large intestine, bladder, and skin. Chemotherapy is the use of medicines that travel in the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body. It is a type of systemic therapy. Recommended chemotherapy regimens for use with radiation to treat anal cancer include mitomycin and capecitabine, mitomycin and 5-FU, and 5-FU and cisplatin. Local excision instead of chemoradiation may be an option for some slow-growing stage I and II perianal cancers. ground_truth: Surgical procedures used in the management of anal cancer include local excision, abdominoperineal resection (APR), and groin (inguinal lymph node) dissection. Local excision is reserved for select early-stage, low-grade perianal cancers where the tumor is small and well-defined. Abdominoperineal resection (APR) is indicated for cases of anal cancer that are persistent, recurrent, or locally progressive after initial treatment, or when the cancer returns to the anal area. APR is a radical surgery that involves removal of the anus, rectum, and surrounding tissues, resulting in the need for a permanent colostomy, as there is no longer a natural route for stool to exit the body. Groin dissection is performed when there is recurrence of cancer in the inguinal lymph nodes. In some cases, muscle flap reconstruction may be required to aid healing after APR, especially if prior radiation therapy has compromised tissue in the perineal area.

ground_truth: Anal cancer treatments, particularly radiation therapy and chemotherapy, can lead to a range of side effects. These include infertility (due to damage to the ovaries or sperm), bowel dysfunction (such as diarrhea and incontinence), urinary dysfunction (including frequent urination or incontinence), and sexual dysfunction. Additional systemic side effects may include hand-foot syndrome, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, skin irritation, mucositis, low blood cell counts, hearing loss (with cisplatin), and neuropathy (with oxaliplatin). To address the risk of infertility, several fertility preservation options are available and should be discussed prior to treatment. These options include sperm banking (semen cryopreservation), egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation), ovarian tissue banking, and oophoropexy (surgical repositioning of the ovaries to minimize radiation exposure).

ground_truth: The subtypes of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) are primarily classified based on the type of lymphocyte from which the leukemia originates and the maturity of the cells. The two main subtypes are B-cell ALL (B-ALL), which starts in B-cell lymphocytes and is more common, and T-cell ALL (T-ALL), which arises from T-cell lymphocytes. B-ALL is characterized by the proliferation of immature B lymphoblasts, while T-ALL involves immature T lymphoblasts and can cause an enlarged thymus, sometimes leading to breathing difficulties. Rare subtypes include mature B-cell ALL (also known as Burkitt leukemia), which is closely related to Burkitt lymphoma and is treated differently from typical B-ALL. Additionally, when lymphoblasts primarily grow in lymph nodes or the thymus rather than the bone marrow, the disease is referred to as lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma or T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, respectively). Classification also considers immunophenotype and specific genetic or chromosomal changes within the leukemia cells.

ground_truth: Pheochromocytoma, which arises from the adrenal medulla, typically presents with symptoms related to excess catecholamine production, such as high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), and sweating. Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma involves imaging studies like CT or MRI scans, as well as biochemical tests to detect elevated catecholamines or their metabolites. In contrast, adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) originates from the adrenal cortex and can present with a broader spectrum of symptoms, including weight gain, muscle weakness, pink or purple stretch marks, and various hormonal changes such as excess facial hair, hair loss on the head, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, and shrinking testicles. ACC may also cause nonspecific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, abdominal bloating, back pain, fever, loss of appetite, and unintentional weight loss. Diagnostic approaches for ACC are more extensive and may include CT scan, MRI, PET scans (such as FDG-PET/CT or SSTR-PET/CT), blood and biochemical tests to assess hormone levels, genetic testing for hereditary syndromes, and biopsy to confirm malignancy.

ground_truth: Breast cancer subtypes are defined based on their site of origin, degree of invasiveness, and clinical and pathological features. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a noninvasive cancer confined to the milk ducts and classified as stage 0. Invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common type, originates in the ducts and invades surrounding breast tissue. Lobular carcinoma starts in the lobules (milk-producing glands) and can also be invasive. Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) is a rare and aggressive subtype characterized by cancer cells blocking lymph vessels in the skin, leading to symptoms such as redness, swelling, warmth, peau d’orange (dimpled skin), and rapid progression; it is typically diagnosed at stage III or IV. Metastatic breast cancer (MBC) refers to cancer that has spread beyond the breast to distant organs (stage IV). Staging incorporates tumor size, lymph node involvement, and presence of metastasis, and is essential for prognosis and treatment planning. Each subtype has unique clinical presentations, pathological findings, and implications for management.

Stage 0 (ductal carcinoma in situ, DCIS) is noninvasive and typically managed with surgery (such as lumpectomy or mastectomy) and may include radiation therapy to reduce recurrence risk. Stages I-III represent invasive breast cancer, where the tumor has spread beyond the ducts or lobules and may involve regional lymph nodes. Treatment for these stages is multimodal and may include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive tumors, HER2-targeted therapy for HER2-positive cancers, and immunotherapy in select cases. Stage IV (metastatic) breast cancer indicates that the disease has spread to distant organs. Management at this stage focuses on systemic therapies such as chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, HER2-targeted agents, and other targeted therapies, with an emphasis on controlling disease progression, alleviating symptoms, and improving quality of life through palliative interventions. Staging is determined using the TNM system and guides both prognosis and individualized treatment planning.

Endocrine therapy is indicated for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, targeting tumors that express estrogen or progesterone receptors. HER2-targeted therapies are used for HER2-positive breast cancers, which overexpress the HER2 protein. PARP inhibitors are prescribed for patients with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations who have HER2-negative breast cancer. CDK4/6 inhibitors are used in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancers to inhibit cell cycle progression. PIK3CA inhibitors are specifically used for PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. These targeted therapies are selected based on the results of molecular and genetic testing, allowing for personalized treatment approaches.

**Patient Presentation:** New referral for a suspicious facial lesion.

- Fair skin, red/blond hair, or light eye color (melanin deficiency increases UV vulnerability).

- **Prevention:** Advise strict sun protection (SPF 30+ sunscreen, protective clothing).

Consult Note:

A new patient was referred for evaluation of a suspicious lesion on the left cheek. Key risk factors for basal cell carcinoma (BCC) in this patient include significant cumulative sun exposure, fair skin phenotype, and a personal history of skin cancer. On physical examination, the lesion is located on a sun-exposed area of the face and appears as a shiny, pearly papule with rolled borders, consistent with classic BCC morphology.

Diagnostic steps will follow current clinical practice guidelines and include: (1) a comprehensive skin examination to assess for additional lesions, (2) a detailed medical and family history to identify further risk factors or hereditary syndromes, and (3) a skin biopsy of the lesion to establish a definitive diagnosis. Imaging studies may be considered if there is clinical suspicion for perineural invasion or deep tissue involvement.

If the diagnosis of BCC is confirmed, the initial management plan will prioritize surgical excision, which is the standard first-line treatment. The patient will be counseled regarding the risk of recurrence and the importance of ongoing surveillance, including annual full skin examinations, as recommended by current guidelines. Additional education will be provided on sun protection and self-skin examination to reduce future risk.

Dear Colleague,

I am referring a patient with a history of basal cell carcinoma (BCC) who now presents with a recurrence at the original site and clinical evidence of regional lymph node involvement. Clinical findings include a recurrent lesion at the prior excision site and palpable lymphadenopathy. The patient possesses several risk factors for BCC, including fair skin, significant ultraviolet (UV) exposure, and a prior personal history of skin cancer. Diagnostic confirmation was achieved through a combination of thorough medical and family history, physical and skin examination, a confirmatory biopsy of the recurrent lesion, and imaging studies to assess the extent of lymph node involvement. According to NCCN guidelines, recurrence and regional spread of BCC represent a higher-risk scenario that may require multimodal management. The rationale for referral is to evaluate the need for systemic therapy or radiation, as these options are recommended for cases where surgical management alone may be insufficient. Further staging and treatment planning are requested in accordance with current evidence-based guidelines.

The sample is sent to a lab to be tested for cancer cells. Tests after diagnosis After an MRI scan and a stereotactic biopsy have confirmed a diagnosis of lymphoma in the central nervous system, a few more tests are needed to find out how far the cancer has grown in the CNS and if it may have spread to other areas of the body. Although many people with primary CNS lymphoma have only one visible tumor, others have multiple tumors on their scan. Testing after diagnosis also checks for signs of cancer in the eyes, cerebrospinal fluid, blood, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and possibly the bone marrow and testicles. Lumbar puncture Cancer cells in the spinal fluid may or may not cause symptoms. A lumbar puncture is used to learn whether cancer has spread to the spinal cord. First, the lower back is numbed. Then a long, thin needle is inserted into the lower part of the spinal column to remove cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid is then sent to a lab for testing. More imaging It’s uncommon for primary CNS lymphoma to spread outside of the central nervous system or the eyes. Still, it’s important to have a look at the rest of your body just to be sure. The imaging methods most commonly used for this are positron emission tomography (PET) and/ or computed tomography (CT). PET imaging uses a small amount of a radioactive drug to find cancer cells in the body. After the radioactive drug is injected into a vein, it causes cancer cells to show up as bright spots on PET scans. A CT scan takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. A computer combines all the x-ray pictures to make a single detailed image.

Induction Phase:
- Initiate high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy, which is the cornerstone of induction therapy for primary CNS lymphoma due to its ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and effectively target lymphoma cells in the CNS.
- Add rituximab, a monoclonal antibody targeting CD20, to enhance treatment response, as it is the primary immunotherapy agent used in this setting.
- Additional agents such as temozolomide or vincristine may be incorporated into the regimen based on established protocols and individual patient tolerance.
- Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) should be used as needed to reduce cerebral edema and alleviate neurological symptoms, but should be tapered as soon as feasible to avoid masking disease activity.

Consolidation Phase:
- After achieving remission or maximal response to induction therapy, proceed to consolidation. The most commonly used approach is whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), which aims to eradicate residual disease and reduce the risk of relapse.
- Alternatively, for selected patients with good performance status, high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous hematopoietic stem cell rescue may be considered, particularly to minimize long-term neurotoxicity associated with WBRT.

- Throughout all phases, provide comprehensive supportive care to manage treatment-related side effects, prevent infections, and address neurological and cognitive symptoms. This includes regular monitoring of renal function (due to high-dose methotrexate), hydration, leucovorin rescue, and management of cytopenias.
- Engage a multidisciplinary team—including neurology, oncology, nursing, pharmacy, and supportive services—to optimize patient outcomes and quality of life.
- Assess performance status regularly to guide treatment intensity and eligibility for clinical trials, which should be considered for all patients given the rarity and complexity of primary CNS lymphoma.

This approach is consistent with current guidelines and evidence, aiming to maximize disease control while minimizing toxicity and preserving neurological function.

Primary CNS lymphoma is a rare, aggressive cancer affecting the brain, spinal cord, or cerebrospinal fluid. **Risk factors** include immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV/AIDS, organ transplants, autoimmune diseases like lupus), Epstein-Barr virus infection, and advanced age (most cases occur in 60s–70s). **Key symptoms** involve neurological deficits (arm/leg weakness, coordination issues, personality changes, memory loss), cognitive decline, vision disturbances (blurred/double vision), and systemic symptoms like headaches, nausea, or seizures. ground_truth:
Public Health Advisory: Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma (PCNSL)

Primary CNS lymphoma is a rare but aggressive cancer that originates from lymphocytes within the central nervous system, most commonly affecting the brain but also the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and eyes. Individuals at increased risk include those with impaired immune systems, such as patients with immunodeficiency disorders, HIV infection, Epstein-Barr virus, autoimmune diseases, organ transplants, and older adults.

Key symptoms to watch for include leg or arm weakness, difficulties with coordination or movement, changes in personality or behavior, memory problems, headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and vision changes such as blurry or double vision. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for improving outcomes. Diagnostic evaluation includes neurological examination, MRI with gadolinium contrast, stereotactic biopsy, laboratory tests, eye examination, and lumbar puncture.

Prompt referral to a neuro-oncology specialist is essential for timely diagnosis and initiation of evidence-based therapy, which typically involves high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy and possible whole-brain radiation therapy. Participation in clinical trials and supportive care are also recommended. Early detection and specialist management can significantly impact patient prognosis.

The patient has a history of chronic sun exposure and presented with a 2.5 cm solid, irregular lesion on an area of chronic scarring. Sincerely,
Dermatology Attending

Discharge Summary for Regional Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (CSCC)

Diagnosis: You have been diagnosed with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) that had spread to a nearby lymph node, which is known as regional CSCC. Major risk factors for this type of skin cancer include chronic sun exposure and a weakened immune system.

Treatment: Your treatment included surgery to remove both the skin tumor and the affected lymph node(s). After surgery, you received radiation therapy to the area to help lower the risk of the cancer coming back. Imaging tests after treatment did not show any further spread of the cancer.

Risk Factors: The main risk factors for CSCC are long-term sun exposure, a weakened immune system, and a history of chronic wounds or scarring. These factors can increase the chance of developing skin cancer or having it return.

Follow-up Plan: Regular follow-up is important to monitor for any signs of recurrence. You will have skin and lymph node checks every 2–3 months during the first year after treatment, then every 2–4 months in the second year, and less frequently in the following years. Imaging may be used as part of your ongoing surveillance. Please continue to protect your skin from the sun and promptly report any new or changing skin lesions to your care team.

Thank you for your cooperation and commitment to your follow-up care.

Public Health Advisory: Prevention and Early Detection of Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (CSCC)

Primary care providers should be vigilant for CSCC, the second most common skin cancer, particularly in fair-skinned individuals and those with extensive sun exposure. High-risk populations include patients with chronic sun exposure, indoor tanning history, actinic keratosis, genetic syndromes (e.g., xeroderma pigmentosum, RDEB), immunosuppression, and chronic wounds or scars. 

Early detection relies on clinical examination for scaly patches or misshapen skin lesions, especially in sun-exposed or chronically damaged areas. Biopsy is essential for suspicious lesions. Encourage sun protection and routine skin exams, especially for high-risk patients. Prompt referral for dermatologic evaluation is recommended for new, persistent, or changing lesions.

ground_truth: For a patient with suspected chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), the diagnostic workup should be comprehensive and systematic. I would begin with a detailed medical history and physical examination, including assessment for symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and splenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation would start with a complete blood count (CBC) with differential to identify leukocytosis, particularly increased granulocytes, and to assess platelet and red blood cell levels. A peripheral blood smear would be performed to evaluate the spectrum of granulocyte maturation and to detect any abnormal or immature cells. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy would be considered to assess cellularity, myeloid proliferation, and the percentage of blasts, which is critical for distinguishing between chronic, accelerated, and blast phases of CML. Cytogenetic analysis (karyotyping) would be performed to detect the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph), resulting from the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) would be used to confirm the presence of the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, which is required for a definitive diagnosis. The disease phase is characterized by the proportion of blasts in blood or marrow: chronic phase (<10% blasts), accelerated phase (10–19% blasts), or blast phase (≥20% blasts). This integrated approach confirms the diagnosis, distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative neoplasms, and guides subsequent management.

ground_truth: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer caused by the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, which arises from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, forming the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph). Diagnosis is established by detecting either the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, typically via cytogenetic and molecular testing of blood or bone marrow samples. The disease originates in blood stem cells, leading to excessive production of myeloid progenitor cells and increased granulocyte (white blood cell) counts, often accompanied by abnormal platelet levels. The primary therapeutic approach targets the BCR::ABL1 protein, whose abnormal tyrosine kinase activity drives disease progression. Initiation of treatment with a BCR::ABL1 protein inhibitor is recommended as first-line therapy for chronic phase CML, with ongoing monitoring of molecular response.

**Public Health Advisory: The Role of Genetic and Molecular Testing in CML Diagnosis**

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer defined by a specific genetic alteration: the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, formed by a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, leading to the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph). Accurate diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation of either the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene through cytogenetic and molecular testing of blood or bone marrow samples. These tests distinguish CML from other blood disorders and are critical for selecting appropriate therapy. Targeted treatments that inhibit the BCR::ABL1 protein have dramatically improved outcomes. Public health initiatives should ensure access to advanced molecular diagnostics for all suspected CML patients.

ground_truth:
Community Health Advisory: Preventing and Detecting Lung Cancer Early

Lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most common type. The primary risk factor for lung cancer is tobacco smoking, but exposure to secondhand smoke, radon, asbestos, air pollution, and certain occupational hazards (such as diesel fumes) also increase risk. While anyone can develop lung cancer, individuals with a history of heavy smoking or significant exposure to these risk factors are at higher risk and should discuss lung cancer screening with their healthcare provider. Screening, such as low-dose CT scans, is recommended for those at high risk and can detect lung cancer at an early, more treatable stage—often before symptoms appear. Early symptoms may include a persistent cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, or unexplained weight loss. Quitting smoking and minimizing exposure to harmful substances are the most effective ways to reduce your risk. Regular checkups, updating your healthcare provider on your family and exposure history, and being aware of new or persistent respiratory symptoms are important for early detection. Participation in clinical trials and supportive care services may also improve outcomes for those diagnosed with lung cancer.

Dear Oncology Team,

I am referring a 45-year-old male of Southeast Asian origin with clinical suspicion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Relevant risk factors include his geographic background, as NPC is more prevalent in individuals from Southeast Asia, and a history of tobacco and alcohol use, both of which are established risk factors for head and neck cancers. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is a major etiologic factor in NPC, and should be considered in this case.

Preliminary findings include the presence of a neck mass, intermittent hearing loss, and an enlarged cervical lymph node on examination. These symptoms are consistent with NPC, which often presents with lymphadenopathy and may cause hearing loss due to Eustachian tube dysfunction. Early-stage NPC can be asymptomatic, so these findings warrant prompt investigation.

The recommended diagnostic workup includes:
- Comprehensive medical history and physical examination, with attention to risk factors and family history.
- Imaging studies: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the head and neck to assess the primary tumor and nodal involvement, and PET/CT to evaluate for distant metastases.
- Biopsy: Histopathological confirmation via biopsy of the nasopharyngeal lesion and/or fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), or core needle biopsy (CNB) of the cervical lymph node.
- Biomarker testing: Assessment for EBV DNA, PD-L1, and MSI-H/dMMR status, as these may inform prognosis and therapeutic options.

Initial management considerations include evaluation of performance status to guide treatment planning, and discussion of fertility preservation options prior to initiation of therapy, as treatment may impact fertility. Dental and nutritional assessments are also advised due to the potential effects of head and neck cancer treatment on oral health and nutritional status. Please proceed with the recommended workup and multidisciplinary evaluation.

**Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC): Multidisciplinary Clinical Protocol**

1. Initial Assessment:
   - Obtain a comprehensive medical history, including geographic origin (notably Asia, Native America, North Africa), family history, and risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol use, and potential EBV exposure.
   - Document all current symptoms, including neck mass, hearing loss, nasal obstruction, or other head and neck complaints, recognizing that early NPC may be asymptomatic.

2. Physical Examination:
   - Perform a thorough head and neck examination, including nasopharyngeal fiberoptic endoscopy and assessment for cervical lymphadenopathy.

3. Diagnostic Workup:
   - Imaging: Order contrast-enhanced CT and/or MRI of the head and neck to assess the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes. PET/CT should be considered to evaluate for distant metastases. Ultrasound may be used to guide lymph node biopsy.
   - Biopsy: Obtain tissue diagnosis via biopsy of the nasopharyngeal lesion and/or fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), or core needle biopsy (CNB) of suspicious lymph nodes. If metastases are suspected, biopsy of metastatic sites should be performed as appropriate.

4. Biomarker Evaluation:
   - At diagnosis, perform biomarker testing for EBV DNA (plasma or tumor), MSI-H/dMMR, PD-L1, HPV, and tumor mutational burden, as these may inform prognosis and therapeutic decision-making.

5. Staging:
   - Utilize the AJCC TNM system to classify tumor size (T), nodal involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).
   - Categorize disease as resectable, unresectable, locoregional, locally advanced, or metastatic based on imaging and clinical findings.

6. Multidisciplinary Review and Initial Management Planning:
   - Present the case at a multidisciplinary tumor board to review diagnostic findings and determine optimal management.
   - Assess performance status to guide treatment selection.
   - Conduct dental and nutritional evaluations prior to therapy due to the potential impact of treatment on oral health and nutrition.
   - Discuss fertility preservation options with the patient before initiating therapy, as treatment may affect fertility.

7. Surveillance and Follow-up Planning:
   - Develop a surveillance plan including periodic physical examinations and imaging (CT, MRI, or PET/CT) as clinically indicated, particularly in the first 5 years post-treatment.
   - Schedule serial EBV DNA testing for early detection of recurrence.
   - Adjust follow-up intervals based on individual risk of recurrence and patient-specific factors.

This protocol ensures a comprehensive, evidence-based approach to the diagnosis, staging, biomarker evaluation, and surveillance of NPC, facilitating coordinated multidisciplinary care.
